source.title: Detecting noisy labels using checkpoint ensembles

record.file_problem: The full 26-page paper is present. Some equations and table layouts are garbled in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test loss and accuracy across training epochs and discusses a time-wise double-descent pattern, using a noisy-label training setup and scheduler comparison rather than reproducing the original study's method.
record.gate_note: The paper's own scheduler experiments and epoch-wise test metrics bear on V2. Its model-size and training-sample-size results are not studied. Cited double-descent results are not recorded as findings of this paper.
record.test_reason: The study's own curves of test loss and accuracy over epochs (ResNet-18, CIFAR-100, 20% uniform label noise) show time-wise double descent, and the authors note it. The new element is a comparison across learning-rate schedules. The evidence is figure-only, from a single run, and incidental to the paper's noise-detection aim. It is a new setting, not the original's method, so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as far as it goes. The authors' main conclusion is that checkpoint ensembles near the early-stopping point (ES-Prediction, ES-BGSS, Plateau) give competitive noisy-label detection. On double descent, they say the best-generalizing checkpoint under continuous schedules can come after memorization, so the first early-stopping point should be used; they recommend a multistep scheduler, under which these points coincide.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tracks test metrics over training time in noisy-label classification and compares learning-rate schedules; it does not reproduce the original double-descent size or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported time-wise behavior differs with learning-rate schedule: it is especially visible for the linear schedule, and the restarted cosine schedule is described as behaving similarly.
record.problems: The scheduler experiment is presented for one setup: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with 20% uniform label noise. The epoch-wise metric values are shown only in figures, without numeric values in the text; the paper also states that presented metrics are based on a single run in each setup.
record.rows_left_out: Noise-detection metrics and comparisons among detection methods are not rows because they do not measure test error over training time. No claim-relevant results were omitted.

untested.parts: No numeric curve values; no variation of model size or noise level for the epoch-wise curve; no noise-free control; single run; only one dataset and architecture for the scheduler study.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
Noise rate is not varied for test-error curves; regularization is not tuned to remove the peak.

missing.what: Statement that under a well-calibrated multistep scheduler the early-stopping, best noise-detection and best task-accuracy checkpoints coincide. This implies the scheduler choice suppresses a beneficial second descent.

record.verdict_notes: Double descent is incidental here: one paragraph, with the observation attributed to Nakkiran et al. [37]. The curves include label noise, as in the original setup. The authors state that the qualitative scheduler behaviour is similar on other tasks, but they show only CIFAR-100. The reader's T2 was changed to T3.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error peak near an interpolation threshold.
No numeric epoch-wise curve values are reported in the text; model-size and sample-size axes are not tested.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
The paper varies label-noise settings for noise detection, but does not test whether noise or regularization drives, splits, or removes a double-descent peak.
No comparison using an effective parameter count.

tranche.reason: The study reports its own epoch trajectories in a noisy-label detection setting and compares learning-rate schedules. Double descent is an incidental empirical finding rather than the principal research question.

source_check.notes: Curve shapes cannot be reconstructed from the extracted figures; R1–R2 rest on the authors' qualitative descriptions. Early stopping uses noisy held-out validation loss with 20-epoch patience and, for multistep scheduling, waits until at least the first learning-rate drop.

statements.correction: ResNet-18; CIFAR-100; 20% uniform label noise; multistep learning rate divided by 10 after epochs 100 and 150; early stopping and best task accuracy coincide; absence of a later shallower descent is not established.
statements.problem: R3 does not support the listed interventions or establish that epoch-wise double descent disappears. This study compares learning-rate schedules; the other studies' claims are outside this check.
